experiences/brazil-pentecostal-belem-191: Pentecostal beginnings in Belém and Brazil's Pentecostal growth
Belém, Pará

Paraphrase of Assembleias de Deus histories: two Swedish Baptist immigrants from Chicago, Gunnar Vingren and Daniel Berg, came to Belém in 1910 after a prophecy naming 'Pará'. In June 1911 Celina de Albuquerque, a member of the Baptist church where they worshipped, was reported to be the first in Brazil to speak in tongues; the Pentecostal group was expelled and formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed Assembleia de Deus in 1918. Healing became a hallmark of later Brazilian Pentecostalism, from the 1950s tent crusades to the neo-Pentecostal Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (founded 1977).

Early Brazilian Pentecostals faced Catholic opposition and were largely poor and urban; today the Assemblies of God in Brazil is one of the largest Pentecostal bodies in the world, and evangelicals were over a fifth of Brazil's population by the 2010 census, most of them Pentecostal.
Pentecostal
Brazilian Pentecostalism is a central example of the global South's 'Spirit-filled' Christianity, with healing and deliverance as means of evangelism.
Catholic
Catholic bishops (e.g. at the Aparecida conference, 2007) responded to losses to Pentecostalism; Catholic Charismatic Renewal grew strongly in Brazil.
Reformed / evangelical critics
Criticise neo-Pentecostal prosperity teaching and commercialisation of healing (especially in the Universal Church).
Sociologist
Andrew Chesnut argues Pentecostalism grows by offering healing from the 'pathogens of poverty' (illness, alcoholism, family breakdown); Paul Freston notes its growing political influence.
Prosperity theology and neo-Pentecostalism.
Pentecostal politics in Brazil.
Healing and poverty.

In the early twentieth century Brazil was overwhelmingly Catholic, with small Protestant communities founded by immigrants and missionaries. Belém, at the mouth of the Amazon in the state of Pará, was a busy port enriched by the rubber boom. Gunnar Vingren and Daniel Berg were young Swedish immigrants to the United States, both from Baptist backgrounds, who had been influenced by the Pentecostal movement spreading through the Midwest, including the ministry of William Durham in Chicago. According to Assembleias de Deus tradition, at a prayer meeting in 1910 a prophecy was given that they should go to a place called 'Pará'. Neither knew where it was until they found it in a library atlas.

The two men sailed for Brazil and arrived in Belém on 19 November 1910 with almost no money and no knowledge of Portuguese. They were welcomed into the local Baptist church, worshipping in its basement while learning the language. Berg worked in a foundry and paid for Vingren's language lessons, while also selling Bibles. They began to share their beliefs about baptism in the Holy Spirit and healing with Baptist members, holding prayer meetings in homes.

According to the church's histories, in early June 1911 a church member, Celina de Albuquerque, after days of prayer, began to speak in tongues, the first such experience recorded in the movement in Brazil, and was reportedly healed of an illness. Others followed. The Baptist pastor and leadership opposed the new teaching, and on 13 June 1911 the Pentecostal group, about eighteen people, was excluded from the church. On 18 June 1911 they began meeting separately as the Apostolic Faith Mission, the date now celebrated as the founding of the Assembleias de Deus. The name was changed to Assembleia de Deus in 1918.

The movement spread first along the Amazon and through the poor north and north-east, carried by lay members who migrated in search of work. It grew among the poor, many of them rural migrants to the cities, and faced opposition from Catholic clergy and sometimes violence from local populations. Swedish Pentecostal churches, especially Lewi Pethrus's Filadelfia church in Stockholm, sent missionaries and support. Vingren returned to Sweden in 1932 in poor health and died in 1933; Berg continued until his death in 1963. Meanwhile another Pentecostal stream, the Congregação Cristã no Brasil, had been founded in São Paulo in 1910 by the Italian immigrant Luigi Francescon, also influenced by Durham.

Healing was central from the start. In the 1950s, a second wave of Pentecostalism came with mass healing campaigns in tents and stadiums by the Foursquare Church's National Evangelisation Crusade, and new Brazilian churches such as O Brasil para Cristo (1955) and Deus é Amor (1962). From the late 1970s neo-Pentecostal churches, above all Edir Macedo's Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977, combined healing, exorcism and prosperity teaching with media empires. The sociologist R. Andrew Chesnut, studying Pentecostals in Belém itself, found that experiences of healing of illness, often related to poverty, were the main reason most converts gave for joining.

By the 2010 census, evangelicals made up about 22 percent of Brazil's population, the majority of them Pentecostal, and the Assembleias de Deus had become one of the largest Pentecostal church families in the world, with many millions of members.

The small group in Belém became the seed of the largest Pentecostal movement in the world by number of adherents in a single country, transforming Brazilian religion, society and politics. Brazilian Pentecostalism shows how healing, especially among the poor, has driven Pentecostal growth in the Global South, and its later neo-Pentecostal forms have exported prosperity theology and media-driven churches to Africa, Europe and beyond. Critics, Catholic and Protestant, have questioned prosperity teaching, financial practices and the growing political power of evangelical blocs in Brazil's Congress. Supporters stress the dignity, community and moral transformation these churches have brought to millions of poor Brazilians.
experiences/chinese-house-church-healing: Healing and growth in Chinese house churches
Henan province, China

Paraphrase of field studies and testimonies: during and after the Cultural Revolution, when public churches were closed, Protestant house-church networks grew rapidly in rural provinces such as Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang. Surveys and interviews from the 1980s-2000s repeatedly found that experiences of healing from illness, often after prayer by lay evangelists, or deliverance from spirits, were among the most common reasons given for conversion. Networks such as Fangcheng and Tanghe sent itinerant evangelists across China.

Chinese authorities often treated unregistered groups as illegal and sometimes labelled healing practices as 'superstition'; registered Three-Self churches tended to be more cautious about healing. Some sectarian groups arising from the same milieu (e.g. Eastern Lightning) were rejected by house churches as heretical.
Chinese house church
Healing and answered prayer are read as signs of the living God's power under persecution, in line with Acts.
Three-Self / registered Protestant
Often more cautious, emphasising rational faith and order, while acknowledging prayer for the sick.
Pentecostal / charismatic
Cited as among the largest examples of 'signs and wonders' evangelism in the world, though many house churches do not identify as Pentecostal.
Historian / sociologist
Healing claims are hard to verify; scholars explain their importance by limited rural healthcare, folk-religious expectations and the social support of house churches. Growth estimates vary widely.
Verification of healing claims and growth statistics.
Heterodox sects arising in the same networks.
State control and 'superstition'.

When the Communist Party took power in China in 1949, there were perhaps around one million Protestants and three million Catholics in the country. Foreign missionaries were expelled by the early 1950s, and Protestant churches were brought under the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, founded in 1954, which required loyalty to the new state. Leaders who refused, such as Watchman Nee and Wang Mingdao, were imprisoned. During the Cultural Revolution (1966-76) all public churches were closed, Bibles were confiscated, and believers were persecuted.

Yet Christian faith did not disappear. In villages across rural China, especially in provinces such as Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang, small groups met secretly in homes to pray, sing and read from whatever Scripture they had. Leadership passed largely to lay people, many of them women. According to later testimonies and field research, these groups often spread through networks of family and neighbours, and stories of prayer for the sick and of answered prayer played a central role.

After the death of Mao Zedong and the beginning of reforms in 1978, registered churches reopened from 1979, and the extent of the growth of Christianity became visible. Researchers and visiting Christians found that many rural communities had far more believers than before 1949. In interviews and surveys from the 1980s to the 2000s, healing was repeatedly named as one of the most common reasons for conversion: a family member's recovery from illness after prayer, often in areas where medical care was scarce or unaffordable, or deliverance from what was experienced as spirit possession. Some local studies suggested that a majority of converts in particular areas cited healing.

Large networks of unregistered house churches emerged, especially in Henan, such as the Fangcheng network associated with Zhang Rongliang, the Tanghe network (China Gospel Fellowship), and the Word of Life movement of Xu Yongze, sometimes called the 'Born Again' movement. They trained young itinerant evangelists who travelled across the country, often facing arrest, imprisonment and beatings. Their worship was fervent, with tears, extended prayer and expectation of signs and wonders, and some networks developed a vision, known as 'Back to Jerusalem', of sending missionaries westward across Asia.

The state's response varied over time and region. Unregistered groups were often treated as illegal gatherings, and officials sometimes condemned healing practices as 'superstition' or 'illegal medical practice'. Registered Three-Self churches were generally more cautious about healing and charismatic practices. The same environment also produced groups regarded as heretical by house churches and the state alike, such as Eastern Lightning (the Church of Almighty God), founded in the early 1990s, which teaches that Christ has returned as a Chinese woman and which house-church networks accused of infiltrating and kidnapping their leaders.

Estimates of the total number of Protestants in China vary widely, from around 23 million in official surveys to 60 million or more in some outside estimates. Scholars such as Alan Hunter, Kim-Kwong Chan and Lian Xi have stressed that this growth took place largely without missionaries, through Chinese lay leadership and a popular Christianity that emphasised prayer, healing and the experience of God's power in daily life.

The growth of Chinese house churches is one of the most remarkable developments in modern Christian history, producing one of the world's largest Protestant populations under a hostile state and without foreign missionary leadership. It shows how healing and experiences of spiritual power can drive conversion in contexts of poverty and limited medical care, a pattern also seen in Africa and Latin America. Critics and scholars point to the difficulty of verifying healing claims and growth statistics, the vulnerability of such networks to heretical sects, and the tensions between registered and unregistered churches. Their story remains central to debates about church and state, religious freedom and indigenous Christianity in China.
